The remaster of The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a nostalgic journey that modernizes a classic RPG while retaining its quirky charm. After over 80 hours of gameplay, the improvements in UI, leveling system, and graphics are evident, making the nearly 20-year-old game feel fresh. The graphical overhaul is particularly impressive, with enhanced lighting and draw distances, although some character models remain cartoonish.

The remaster introduces a sprint button, significantly improving exploration speed, and modernizes the UI for better navigation. However, the leveling system still suffers from the frustrating enemy scaling that plagued the original, making it feel unfair at times. While the game excels in its freedom and intricate quest design, it does have flaws, particularly in NPC interactions and AI, which can detract from immersion.

Despite these shortcomings, Oblivion's stunning graphics, compelling narrative, and the sheer variety of experiences make it a standout title in the series. The engaging faction quests and whimsical spellcrafting system offer a unique experience that stands out in the RPG genre. Overall, Oblivion Remastered is a delightful return to Cyrodiil, blending nostalgia with modern gameplay enhancements, though it still carries some of the original's quirks. Players will find themselves lost in the enchanting world of Cyrodiil, where every choice leads to unexpected adventures, solidifying Oblivion as a bold and ambitious RPG that remains a beloved classic.

[b]PROS:[/b]
+ epic world to explore
+ cool quests
+ many fun RPG elements
+ mods, fixes, wiki pages
+ incredible community

[b]CONS:[/b]
- weird levelling system
- quest breaking issues
- a Bethesda amount of bugs, glitches & crashes
- inventory clutter

[b]Comment:[/b]
The playtime here does not even slightly reflect the unholy amount of time I spent with this game since 2007. Oblivion looks weird at times, everyone is a potato head, stuff clips through other stuff, something is too radiant while something is close to invisible. Voice acting is mostly terrible (not you Patrick Stewart, I love you). And despite that, or because of it, it has an undeniable fantasy charm that grips and holds you.

Main story is simple but cool. But the myriad of side quests is what gives the province of Cyrodiil it's true flavour. The huge variety of style is what makes this game fantastic. From fetch quests to intricate stealth mission to grand combat. You have it all here. My personal favourite is closing all of the oblivion gates. This was even expanded upon with the Knights of the Nine expansion and the marvellous Shivering Isles expansion.

It is a Bethesda game so the bugs and glitches are there of course, when it is not modded. There is a lot of crashing to desktop, especially with a big number of mods, so definitely save often. Quests break, NPCs just die or items disappear, so SAVE OFTEN. This is also the company that introduced the legendary horse armor DLC that brought with it the endless tide of useless DLCs and microtransactions.

So why do so many, including me, like it? Well, as mentioned, it was the freedom you would have while playing. Being able to do whatever in the game world you wanted to do. The community that was built around this game is legendary and definitely why it is thought of so fondly. If you did not know what to do or where to go you hopped onto UESP and got all your info, including console commands to fix broken or missing stuff. And just to list my favourite mods - Three unofficial patches (base game, Shivering Isles, DLC) that fix a HUUUUGE load of issues. Keychain to remove some inventory clutter. Oblivion XP to remake the levelling system into something more engaging and intuitive. There are many other cool mods you can go through on various sites (like Nexus Mods) and tune your experience.

It's an old game that stands on the shoulders of the modding community so get it on a good sale. But it is definitely worth checking out if you are even a bit into RPG games!

[b]P.S.:[/b] You probably already own this game but if you do not then GET THE GOTY DELUXE EDITION. Because once you own the GOTY version (base game+Knights of the Nine+Shivering Isles) it might not let you to buy the Deluxe upgrade. That means you would miss out on these DLCs:
[list]
[*]Fighter's Stronghold
[*]Spell Tome Treasures
[*]Vile Lair
[*]Mehrune's Razor
[*]The Thieves Den
[*]Wizard's Tower
[*]Orrery
[*]Horse Armor Pack
[/list]
And while these are not full expansions it would be a shame to not get the whole Oblivion package. Even if the versioning of this all is stupid...

[b]P.S.2:[/b] A remaster is available now that fixes some of the things listed as CONS and can be found [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2623190/The_Elder_Scrolls_IV_Oblivion_Remastered/]HERE[/url]. Unfortunately, the optimization of it stands to be criticized for poor performance and constant crashes. So for some people this original version with mods has to be the answer if they want to play.

My PC Master Race Pro LRGBT Gaming Setup (six years old Lenovo laptop) is practically powered by pleading, begging, praying, crying, virgin blood sacrifices, and gentle head pats. So naturally, when the remaster came out, I came. Out. Of a closet. Because I slept there. Because I was drunk as hell. The night before. And the night before. Also, I live in that closet. But also also, arguably more importantly maybe probably, the remaster reminded me of when I was a little kid, stepping out of the sewers into the magical, colorful world for the first time. The sun! The trees! The water! The strangers, which I immediately murdered! Then, I made my way into civilization and played Oblivion. And now, years in prison later, after I realized no amount of head pats will convince my machine to run the remaster, I thought to myself - what the heck! Let's rip this bad boy open and relive some of that sweet, sweet nostalgia!

Of course, as with any RPG including a character creator, I pondered quite a bit about whether to make a brainass charizard wizard, or sneaky snickery sneaker. But as always, I went with my comfort zone - ooga booga warfare.  You see, if daycare taught me anything, it's the fact that everything, and I mean EVERYTHING, can be solved with a chunk of wood and/or iron of the size of a horse member! Oh, you're a mighty forest archer, using pinetrees as a funtime toy or whatever? Try to fit in this absolutely humongous warhammer! Ah, you're a great wizard? You've spent thirty years filling that big head of yours with magic? You can cast some quirky lil icicles and fireballsacks? Let's see how many spells you can even remember with your brain being turned into a heap of rotten cabbage! Oh wow, you're a powerful necromancer? You have your cute lil crayon drawings of ancient knowledge? You're about to summon King Lord Demon Snotdrooler The Third Tickler of Devil's Skidmarks? WELL, Let me introduce you and Snotdrooler to my friend Blunt Force Trauma!

Anyway, after half an hour of sliding sliders, rotating rotaters, and fingering buttons, my bastard child, my pride and joy, my vessel for this revolutionary philosophy of mine, was ready to step into the land of Tamriel. That's right! There's new soon-to-be Hero of Kvatch in town. 

Meet Jeff Whackaton. He's but a simple man, with a simple desire - to have a world record in crushed skulls. But he's not a picky one, oh, no. Nords? Sure. Orcs? No problem! Elves of all shapes and colors? Betcha! Undead of all smells and disabilities? Hell yeah! Wildlife? More like notalive! Jeff is not after gold, or fame, or women, or women bought with gold and fame. In fact, even he would have a hard time explaining the motivation driving his mighty hammer onto the heads of his foes. If asked what lies behind those comically tiny eyes of his, he'd stop for a moment, raise his hairy eyebrows, maybe even think. But then, he'd just shrug off those questions with nothing but a grunt and thorough rectum scratch.

But fate had different plans, it seemed. Jeff was in prison for - to keep things family friendly - smashing a random beggar's head so hard that it exploded in million pieces, blood, shrapnels of skull and brain matter washing over nearby citizens, the air quickly filling with the stench of rust and death. Alas, city guards quickly caught our hero, as they were on a cig break like ten feet away, and brought him to the judge, as he was on a booze break like fifteen feet away. Unsurprisingly, they gave Jeff a lengthy sentence. For tax fraud.

Interesting lovely lore aside, one sunny day, Jeff was slav squatting in the corner of his cell, naked, doing a big poopoo, as the good boy he is. Just as he was about to do a big peepee as well, as the good boy he is, the door of his cell burst open, and three people calmly walked in. They were no ordinary people though, they were two not ordinary soldiers AND - the not ordinary Emperor himself! Jeff, a man of ordinary manners, immediately stood up, naked. And then, Emperor said something-something, too long, don't care. And Jeff, oh sweet Jeff, with heart as big as his nose, he looked at the Emperor, naked, and whilst drooling onto his not ordinarily hairy chest, he uttered - "Urrggh."

And so, Jeff's journey began. A journey of self-expression and self-realization. A journey of magic and blades. A journey of talking to the ugliest looking somewhat sapient beings ever rendered in a videogame, picking flowers, caving heads in, and generally being a danger to the ecosystem and society. Where will it end? When will it end? How will it end? And most importantly, will Jeff crush enough skulls before the authorities catch up to him and imprison him for public urination? And tax fraud? Only time will tell. One thing is for sure, though - Jeff Whackaton is packin'. And he'll be whackin'.

So... sure, you can play a wizard, create all sorts of absolutely broken spells. Sure, you can play a thief, steal anything your dirty sausage fingers can press "E" on, and backstab frontstabbers for ridiculous amount of damage. Sure, you can play-pretend an archer (it sucks). And sure, it can be fun. But honestly? We all should be more like Jeff. Be like Jeff. Thoroughly scratch your rectum.

What more is there to say? The answer is nothing. So let me finish this... review... the only way I know, the way I usually finish Oblivion's main quest:

There are games you play, and there are games that shape you. For me, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion wasn’t just my first open-world RPG on PC—it was a revelation. A portal into another realm. A world that became my second home during those impressionable teenage years.

Oblivion opened with a whisper and a storm: a dying emperor, a prison escape, and the faint promise of destiny. But what came after that—stepping out of the sewers and into the sun-drenched heart of Cyrodiil—was a moment I'll never forget. That feeling of complete freedom, the wind brushing through golden fields, the soundtrack swelling with wonder... It was pure magic.

The story was more than just a plot to stop a demonic invasion—it was about identity, choice, and becoming a hero on your own terms. From the eerie mystery of the Dark Brotherhood to the desperate battles at Oblivion gates, every quest felt alive. Every decision, meaningful.

Gameplay-wise, Oblivion struck the perfect balance between accessibility and depth. Its skill system let you mold your character exactly how you wanted, while its factions gave you entire storylines to live out—from noble knight to shadowy assassin. And who could forget that satisfying ka-chunk of landing a sneak attack with a poisoned blade?

But it was the world itself that captured my heart. Rolling hills, ancient ruins overrun by nature, snowy peaks in Bruma, the alien glow of Daedric realms—it was beautiful, eerie, and endlessly explorable. There was always something just over the next hill: a dungeon, a forgotten shrine, a view that made you stop and just exist in the moment.

The music—my god, the music. Jeremy Soule's score wasn’t just background; it breathed with the world. It wrapped around every sunrise, every lonely road, every victory and defeat. It felt like Cyrodiil had a soul.

Years have passed. Games have come and gone. But Oblivion? It stays. It's the kind of game that leaves fingerprints on your memory, the kind you remember not just for what it was, but for who you were when you played it.

Oblivion didn’t just let me escape—it taught me to wander, to imagine, to lose myself in a story. And for that, it will always be my favorite.

The sheer vastness of its world map, the knowledge that any distant peak you saw was indeed reachable was something almost entirely new in the world of 3D open world RPGs. Many nights I found myself spending long hours adventuring through Cyrodiil, lulled to sleep during gameplay by the game's enchanting soundtrack only to wake up walking into a tree before deciding I'd better head to bed.

That was a long time ago however, and I'd have to say that The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion does not hold up so well in 2025. As a setting, Cyrodiil is probably one of the more bland locations in the entire series. Yes it has lush green forests, smoldering Oblivion planes and snowy peaks, but it lacks a certain something to give it the 'character' of Morrowind or Skyrim. For me, Morrowind wins out all with its setting, story and nostalgia factor. Skyrim however is by far the most fun game to play in the series. Oblivion is neither especially fun to play, nor all that nostalgic, and with arguably the least compelling story and player character. I frequently have to remind myself what the player character's title is in the game's lore: The Hero of Kvatch, granted for closing the first Oblivion gate in a small, unimportant town called Kvatch that is already laid to waste by the time you discover it and never gets rebuilt. So you didn't even really save it. It doesn't hold a candle to being Morrowind's Nerevarine or Skyrim's Dragonborn.

Oblivion is not a bad game, but I don't recommend playing it if you aren't already really nostalgic for a time when it actually seemed new and exciting. It just doesn't hold up.

When The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion launched, it felt like the next giant leap for gaming. For me, it was not just about the expansive open world or the deep lore. What truly took my breath away was the first time I witnessed HDR lighting in action.

Stepping out of the sewers after the tutorial and into the open world for the first time was unforgettable. The trees shimmered in the breeze, lakes gleamed in the distance, and the sky itself looked almost too vivid to be real. I remember just standing there, turning the camera slowly, soaking it all in. HDR gave everything a sense of life, of warmth, of a real world breathing beyond the screen.

Oblivion wasn't perfect. Some faces looked strange, and the level scaling could sometimes feel frustrating. But none of that mattered in those first magical moments under the golden sky. Bethesda had built a world that felt like it truly existed, and thanks to HDR, it was bursting with light and color in a way that made exploration irresistible.

Even today, I can still picture that first moment clearly. Crawling out of the darkness into a world bathed in sunlight, with the promise of endless adventures stretching out before me. Oblivion didn’t just introduce me to Cyrodiil --- it introduced me to a new era of beauty in gaming.

Oblivion is one of those rare games that hits you with a sense of adventure the moment you step out of the sewers and into the open world of Cyrodiil. Even all these years later, there's something magical about that first burst of sunlight and the overwhelming freedom that follows. You want to become a noble knight? A sneaky assassin? A walking cheese wheel hoarder? Oblivion says, “Go for it.”
The world is brimming with charm—from the slightly offbeat NPC dialogue to the surprisingly deep questlines like the Dark Brotherhood arc (which is still one of the best in the series). Sure, the graphics are showing their age, and the combat can feel a little clunky by today’s standards, but it somehow adds to the charm. It’s janky in the best, most Bethesda way.
What really makes Oblivion special is how it doesn’t take itself too seriously. It’s epic when it wants to be, but it’s also a playground for chaos, exploration, and experimentation. The character leveling system may have confused more players than it helped, but honestly, who cared when you were having this much fun?
Now, all eyes are on the rumored remaster. If they can polish up the visuals, tweak the systems, and keep that signature Oblivion heart intact, we might just be in for a nostalgic return trip that's better than ever.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion – Game of the Year Edition (GOTY), released in 2009, is a definitive package of one of the most influential Western RPGs of the 2000s. Developed by Bethesda Game Studios and originally launched in 2006, Oblivion marked a generational leap in role-playing game design. The GOTY Edition includes the base game alongside its two major expansions, Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles, offering a massive fantasy experience that blends open-world freedom, deep customization, and richly imaginative storytelling. Even years after its release, Oblivion remains a standout title for both long-time fans of the genre and newcomers seeking an expansive, player-driven adventure.

At the heart of Oblivion is its open-world structure. The game takes place in Cyrodiil, a central province of Tamriel, and presents a lush, diverse landscape filled with dense forests, ancient ruins, misty swamps, snow-covered mountains, and bustling cities. From the outset, players are given immense freedom to forge their own path — whether that means following the central questline, delving into ancient tombs, joining guilds, becoming a vampire, or simply wandering the wilderness in search of hidden treasures. The scale and interactivity of the world were groundbreaking at the time, and while many newer titles have since expanded on its formula, Oblivion's ambition and execution still command respect.

The main storyline follows the player character, known as the Hero of Kvatch, who emerges from prison at the behest of Emperor Uriel Septim (voiced by Patrick Stewart, in a memorable if brief performance). The Empire is crumbling, and the gates to Oblivion — a hellish parallel dimension ruled by Daedric forces — are opening across the land. The hero must track down the Emperor’s last heir and help him reclaim the throne while closing the Oblivion gates that threaten to consume Tamriel. Though the central quest is compelling and filled with iconic set pieces (such as the Siege of Kvatch or the final battle in the Imperial City), it is arguably the least interesting part of the game — which speaks volumes about the richness of everything else surrounding it.

Where Oblivion truly shines is in its faction and guild questlines. The Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood, Mages Guild, and Fighters Guild each have robust story arcs with meaningful choices, unique rewards, and dramatic narrative turns. The Dark Brotherhood, in particular, stands out for its darkly humorous and morally complex missions that involve deception, assassination, and ritual. These questlines often outshine the main story in terms of writing, pacing, and player agency. Each faction feels like a game within the game, and progressing through their ranks is deeply rewarding, both narratively and mechanically.

Character customization and progression in Oblivion are rooted in Bethesda's classic Elder Scrolls formula. Players can create a character from a variety of races, each with distinct attributes and racial abilities, and then choose a class or define their own. Skills improve through use — swinging a sword improves blade skill, sneaking around boosts stealth, casting spells develops magic abilities. This organic leveling system is immersive but not without flaws; the infamous “level scaling” mechanic, where enemy strength rises as the player levels up, can result in absurd situations where lowly bandits wear glass armor or Daedra become more common than wolves. It’s a controversial design choice that can make the game feel punishing if the player doesn't carefully manage their leveling, though mods and certain playstyles can mitigate this issue.

The GOTY Edition includes both Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles, each offering substantial additional content. Knights of the Nine is a more traditional heroic questline centered on divine relics and ancient evils, providing an enjoyable, if relatively straightforward, narrative experience. In contrast, Shivering Isles is a wildly imaginative and surreal expansion set in the realm of Sheogorath, the Daedric Prince of Madness. It introduces an entirely new landscape, distinct aesthetic, and narrative tone — blending humor, horror, and philosophical musings into a bizarre yet captivating experience. The Shivering Isles expansion is often regarded as one of the best pieces of DLC ever made, and it elevates the GOTY Edition into must-play territory.

Visually, Oblivion was revolutionary for its time, with dynamic lighting, expansive draw distances, and detailed environments that pushed the capabilities of the Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and PC platforms. While the graphics haven’t aged perfectly — character models are notoriously stiff and animations awkward by today’s standards — the game’s art direction and environmental design still evoke a strong sense of place and wonder. The forests feel alive, ancient ruins are shrouded in mystery, and the cities have unique architecture and character. Sound design, including Jeremy Soule’s sweeping orchestral score, is a standout, setting the mood for exploration and conflict alike. The voice acting, though limited by a small pool of actors voicing dozens of characters, has a certain nostalgic charm despite its repetition.

Technically, the GOTY Edition benefits from years of patching and improvements over the original 2006 release, though it still carries the quirks and bugs typical of large Bethesda RPGs. Glitches range from harmless oddities to occasional crashes, but the modding community has stepped in to address many of these issues. In fact, the modding scene is a huge part of Oblivion’s longevity — players on PC can access thousands of mods that enhance graphics, fix bugs, overhaul combat, add new content, or even change entire game systems. For many fans, modding is a core part of the Oblivion experience, and the GOTY Edition serves as the ideal foundation for customizing and expanding the game.

In summary, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion – Game of the Year Edition is a sprawling, imaginative, and groundbreaking RPG that still holds up remarkably well more than a decade after its release. While it shows its age in some areas — particularly in combat, animation, and NPC behavior — its vast world, memorable questlines, deep character development, and endless exploration opportunities remain compelling. The included expansions only strengthen its value, making this edition the most complete and rewarding way to experience one of the most influential fantasy RPGs ever made. Whether you’re returning to Cyrodiil for nostalgia or discovering it for the first time, Oblivion GOTY is a timeless journey that continues to inspire the genre to this day.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion - Game of the Year Edition: A Timeless RPG Classic

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion - Game of the Year Edition takes one of the most beloved RPGs of all time and enhances it with added content and features, cementing its place as a must-play title for any fan of open-world exploration and fantasy storytelling. Originally released in 2006, Oblivion continues to be a benchmark in the RPG genre, offering an expansive world, deep lore, and endless possibilities for players seeking adventure, exploration, and role-playing freedom.

The game thrusts players into the heart of Cyrodiil, a rich and vibrant world filled with a variety of environments, from the lush, green landscapes of the Imperial City to the dark and eerie forests and dungeons that hide both danger and treasure. With its breathtaking visuals (for its time), Oblivion set the stage for open-world games to come, offering players a vast, immersive environment to explore at their own pace.

As the player, you are tasked with preventing the obliteration of the world by closing dangerous portals to Oblivion and unraveling the mystery of a dying Emperor. Along the way, you can interact with a wide array of characters, join factions, and engage in countless quests that span the entire game world. Whether you decide to focus on the main storyline or take part in side quests, guilds, and personal stories, the choice is yours, and the game never forces you into any particular path.

The character creation and customization options in Oblivion are exceptional, allowing you to craft a unique hero with various skills, abilities, and magical powers. You can be anything from a warrior, thief, mage, or assassin, each path offering its own strengths and challenges. This level of freedom, along with the ability to role-play as you see fit, gives the game its lasting appeal. The Game of the Year Edition adds even more with its downloadable content (DLC) expansions, including the popular Shivering Isles expansion that introduces new regions, quests, and a deeper story that expands the world and narrative in exciting ways.

Combat in Oblivion is straightforward but satisfying, with players able to wield a variety of weapons, cast powerful spells, and use a range of tactics to defeat enemies. The game’s AI is surprisingly sophisticated, with enemies adapting to your playstyle, and the dynamic weather and day-night cycle add immersion and variety to the world. Whether you’re battling the undead, rogue bandits, or terrifying Daedric creatures, every fight feels like a meaningful encounter.

One of the game’s standout features is its deep lore and world-building. Oblivion is set in the rich Elder Scrolls universe, which is steeped in history and culture. As you explore the game world, you’ll uncover books, artifacts, and characters that flesh out the deep mythology of Tamriel. The Shivering Isles expansion also introduces new gods, realms, and a whole new layer of madness that adds further depth to the experience.

The Game of the Year Edition adds substantial value with its included expansions. Along with Shivering Isles, the edition includes Knights of the Nine, which offers additional story content and quests that expand upon the lore of the game’s world. These expansions further enrich the game’s already vast world, offering even more hours of content and allowing players to experience fresh challenges and locations.

Despite some technical limitations due to its age, Oblivion is a testament to the enduring quality of Bethesda’s RPG design. The AI may seem a little outdated by today’s standards, and some of the mechanics can feel clunky compared to modern RPGs, but the sheer scope and freedom the game offers remain unparalleled. The variety of playstyles, the depth of character development, and the intricacy of the world are what keep players returning to Cyrodiil time and time again.

The soundtrack, composed by Jeremy Soule, is another standout feature of Oblivion. The epic, sweeping scores set the tone for every journey and every battle, enhancing the game’s emotional depth. The music is memorable, timeless, and perfectly complements the vast landscapes and tense moments in the game.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion - Game of the Year Edition is more than just a game; it’s a landmark in RPG history. With its deep world-building, endless exploration, and engaging gameplay, it continues to be an essential experience for anyone who loves open-world adventures. Whether you’re a new player discovering the game for the first time or a long-time fan revisiting Cyrodiil, Oblivion offers a timeless adventure that stands as one of the greatest RPGs ever made.

Experienced years ago, Oblivion is a wonderful game, it is better polished than Morrowind which was great too.  Oblivion adds more of a guided story adventure, a beautiful world, and more voice acted characters to add action sequences and cinematics to the game.  The lush overworld map of castles and caves is intriguing to explore but also adds an other-worldliness factor with the Oblivion Gates that appear through out the land.

Oblivion Gates
Each Oblivion gate is like a mini dimension that you can conquer by exploring the towered structures, killing the demon inhabitants, and eventually removing the Sigil Stone to destroy the infested, infected Gate.
It is so satisfying to conquer these weird dimensions since each one is a different labyrinth of towers, doors and stairs, and you gain valuable items for your efforts.
You become a hero as your close gates, and save the overworld town from the rush of demons that try to overrun the land.

Play
Elder Scrolls games like Oblivion are hard to stay on track to complete because it is so easy to explore multiple hours outside of the main quest.  It always feels like there are places to find, and unknown hovels to explore that "live" outside of the main game.  You need to find people, follow them, and wait for people to be in specific locations. Luckily there is a fast travel method to click on any discovered location on the map, and also you can make time pass by "waiting" in place.
Your time will also be spent fiddling with gear and spells, and sometimes you spend a lot of time healing, recovering magic, and repairing gear from a fight.  You will need to click through many dialog trees and make sure you are not missing an important piece of information.
After a few hundred hours into the game I had set the game aside and I had to force myself to come back and stick to main quest and finally finish the game.

Story
I enjoy this game a lot but I could not recite the story at all, because it was not super important to me.  I closed gates, beat enemies, and quested but the good thing is you do not have to pressure yourself to know every detail.  The game will tell you where to go next in your quest log.  The game is the journey.

BEST on PC (not on Console)
Although I had originally had this game on PlayStation3, I never pursued it very far because a controller is so slow and flipping through the menus are a nightmare. I ended up getting the game for PC, because it is so much more enjoyable to use a keyboard and mouse to control Bethesda games for all the aiming and menus.

Retrospective
Oblivion is a great, immersive game, that can take you away to another place if you allow yourself. It feels more like reading a great adventure book that allows you to proceed at your own pace.  The taste for this style of game ebbs and flows, like watching a slow moving baseball season versus only watching the World series games.  With Oblivion you get the whole season and the championship all in one, if you stay the course.  
At some point I may consider playing the Remastered version, or even the original PC version again, but you need to allow yourself to sit back and chill in a world that brings you to another place.

I also got tired of running into the wild beasts of Cyrodiil: mountain lions, wolves, trolls, etc. because the combat is whack. I thought Skyrim had crap combat that left a lot to be desired... oh lord, Oblivion learned me good. This is even worse. This was, I think, the same issue I had with Far Horizon: the combat is too tedious. I didn't feel like there were incrementally-increasing levels of skill needed to be applied. It's not like KC:D where it's on your understanding of HEMA that you must rely to best your opponents in combat. It's hit-sponges that just take time to kill. Too much time. The stagger mechanic where you're immobilized for a hard few seconds takes even more away from enjoyment. The awful UI forcing you to have to sift through disorganized items and spells did, too.
Again, I don't have any nostalgia factor, and I'm not a high-school teenager with all the time in the world, anymore. That's a 'no' from me with the repetitive leveling grinds. MISS ME with that s**t. I kicked the difficulty level all the way down because combat is just not fun. I'd rather spend an afternoon training with Cpt. Bernard in KC:D than spend 10 minutes in combat here.
"You can talk to trainers for leveling"— yes, indeed, but you're hardcapped to 5 skill level per character level— a scant amount.

One of the activities I love to do in these open-world first-person RPGs like KCD or Skyrim is opt out of fast-traveling to experience the world through actually meandering through the environment, but with combat being as much of a nuisance as it was, I fast-traveled to my heart's content like I was back in RuneScape on a farm run.

Other complaints: 
- hitboxes are arsecheeks. I've missed many spells that go right through the opponent's ribs. If you shoot a spell right in their face, it passes through their body. Come on.
- Way too many game crashes. Late into the game, I got the glitch where items added to the inventory didn't show up until you reloaded your save.
- Oblivion gates quickly became tedious. They're money-dungeons, but beyond that, I quickly came to speedrunning them to just be done with them. No lore or puzzles or anything found in them that kept me engaged. Disappointing.
- UI is garbage. Again, I deeply regret not modding. Inventory is so clumsy and a clusterf**k. Spells are cluttered. Quests are jumbled. Good grief.

There's a lot to like about the game and that's why I stuck with it to complete the main storyline, but overall, I had a mind-numbing experience. If I ever decide to play this again (doubtful), this game will be modded beyond recognition.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is an action RPG developed by Bethesda Game Studios and published by Bethesda Softworks.
Set in the Imperial province of Cyrodiil, you play as a prisoner turned hero, who escapes from prison after you are the only two survivors of a plot to the assassinate Emperor Uriel Septim VII.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*]Graphics look pretty good for their time.
[*]The main story and side content are good, especially the Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood quest lines.
[*]Hundreds of hours of content.
[*]Outstanding world-building.
[*]The game is fairly immersive. You can easily lose track of time while exploring its world, which offers tons of things to discover.
[*]Each city has its own unique look.
[*]Unlike in Skyrim, you can cast spells without having to unequip your weapons and shield.
[*]Spellcrafting, so you can create some absolutely ridiculous spells.
[*]NPCs comment on your skills, which is pretty cool.
[*]Varied types of enemies.
[*]DLCs are really good, except for the infamous Horse Armor DLC.
[*]You can cosplay as the biggest racist in the Elder Scrolls universe, Pelinal Whitestrake.
[*]Fantastic soundtrack.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*]The game has tons of bugs. I recommend installing the unofficial patches.
[*]The game frequently crashes. Save often to avoid losing too much progress.
[*]Really bad pop-in. Entire fortresses and Aylied ruins only appear at close distance. It's probably a limitation of the time, but it's annoying nonetheless.
[*]Character faces are fugly.
[*]Minor skills don't contribute to leveling up.
[*]Level scaling breaks the sense of progression because enemies become much stronger than you. I recommend turning down the difficulty.
[*]The combat is clunky. It really isn't fun to get staggered every few hits.
[*]Both the dungeons and the oblivion gates get repetitive very fast.
[*]Very limited number of voice actors.
[*]Some of the voice lines don't correspond with the subtitles, which are usually correct.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
If, like me, you played Skyrim first, there's a lot here that will be familiar to you.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a fantastic game with great stories and characters, as well as a fantastic world to explore. However, it's not without its faults, as there are a lot of issues.

While the graphics are a bit dated by today's standards, the atmosphere and storytelling still hold up, and with mod support, you can breathe new life into the visuals. The original version of this game honestly holds up better than the remaster imo, for a few key reasons:

1. The remaster is basically in the dark ages of modding right now as of June 2025, the date of this review. There are mods for the game, which are awesome, but no mod manager has been created yet. Sooooo that's a massive issue right out of the gate, largely due to-

2. The remasters insistance of UE5 visuals baked on the LOOOONG dated Gamebryo engine. Which, as I've heard, is horribly optimized for performance. And the remaster is exceptionally bad at performance right now. 

3. The price is better. Admittedly 50 bucks is better than 60, or god forbid EIGHTY, but I was planning to get the remaster for the summer sale. It's 20% off. 20% off a game with no mod manager and shit performance, I'm keeping my hard earned money thank you very much. If it were 50% off or preferably more I MIGHT have gotten it.  Might. The original GOTY deluxe edition is only 20 bucks, runs infinitely better, and has DECADES of mods and a rich history behind it all.

4. Ok now, this is gonna be a hot take. I think the visuals of both the original and the remaster are pretty good in their own right. However, I LOVE the "painted world" aesthetic of the original to death, which the remaster does not have AT ALL. But that isn't exactly a bad thing per se. Just a different visual style.

5. Even minor things like physics, the original does better! If you cast a powerful enough shock spell, anyone hit with it will be sent flying 20 meters across the sky! In the remaster...they just kinda...drop dead....realistically....yeahhhh...I really don't like how they botched up the physics in favor of "rEalIsm!!"...in a fantasy game no less!

6. Now yes, the original absolutely has aged poorly in some aspects. The character models are notoriously ugly, but a key part of Oblivion's charm nonetheless, but there are even worse things, like the leveling system and unbalanced enemies as a result of the leveling system. My biggest gripe with the original was the combat. You always kept getting randomly staggered while enemies move way too fast, and combat generally consists of blocking following by circling the enemy and spamming attack while preventing them from being able to. Power attacks don't stagger enemies unlike in Skyrim, and honestly don't even do that much more damage! The magic system, while MUCH better since you can make your own spells, is also really flawed, and I don't mean the absolute fun you can have in making broken shit, but I mean the unfun aspects, like the strange balancing of certain spells causing them to be underpowered as fuck, (why do bound weapons only last FIFTEEN SECONDS by default? Where are the "on target" Absorb Health spells?!) and some levels of spells not even being present on mages, so you have to make your own. (Drain Fatigue has Novice, Apprentice, and Expert variations, but no Journeyman spells? WTF??) 

Initally I was attracted to the remaster, hyped even! Because it seemed to have finally fixed the combat system and made many QOL changes, enemies even reacted to your attacks, which the original didn't have! But then, the issues kept growing. And growing. And growing! 

I actually went back to my modded original game, and honestly, I had LOADS of fun there! And it actually made me stop...and realize....why did I want the remaster again? C-Can you even CALL it a remaster?! It looks more like a reMAKE to me! Generally the rule of thumb for all Elder Scrolls games is this: If there is something you don't like or something you want for whatever reason, a mod will fix/create it. If it doesn't exist, someone out there will make it. Tbh, I really wish we didn't have to mod our games to fix things like performance or crappy combat systems that really don't hold up today, but alas, that's kinda how it just works, pun very much intended. But yes, the modding community has done great strides in fixing a lot of issues I have with the game, including the combat, thanks to a recent mod. It's FAR from perfect, even in my modded setup, and could use much improvement, but it feels SO much better than vanilla! And hey, if you can appreciate the vanilla game, warts and all, or even genuinely enjoy the original combat system, that's not a bad thing at all! I do appreciate the vanilla game for what it is, and my first experience was Oblivion on the Xbox 360, and I had an awesome time there! Unfortunately, due to my experience with the game, I don't think I can ever go back to pure vanilla. Mods have spoiled me.

The best part about the remaster was actually making me appreciate the original version all the more! Who would've thought?

Oh! Here's something the remaster doesn't have! There's a mod for the original Oblivion where every time a guard says "You have my ear, citizen" they will literally give you one of their ears! 

...as an alchemy ingredient, but honestly, that's even funnier! 

Humor like that is something we need in games today. 

TLDR: Remaster bad, original good, don't waste your time with the remaster and just get the GOTY deluxe edition, you won't regret it

This is a weird recommend from me, because it almost seems like Oblivion is one of those "you had to be there" experiences for millennials. The game is strange -- simultaneously good and bad, beautiful and ugly, at times contemplative, tranquil, and at other times goofy as hell. Rather than recount what so many others already have about the graphics, voice acting, combat system, questlines, The Leveling Problem, etc. etc., I'm just going to say what I like to do in the game these days, after thousands of hours across Steam, GOG, and the Xbox 360.

I think it's a fun dungeon-crawler adventure experience. Through the early game, delving into caves and Ayleid ruins, mowing down bandits and goblins, finding your first silver or enchanted weapon to fight ghosts, and getting those rare enchanted item drops that can make or break your Level 4 build -- that's what I like to do. Selling loot and saving up gold to choose between a horse, a house, a few new spells, or some critical skill training -- those are the decisions I enjoy agonizing over. Doing some odd side quests for innkeepers, merchants, travelers in distress, and eccentric collectors -- that's how I want my adventurer to gain Fame and grow their skills. 

The experience starts to break down as you enter the higher level brackets, and a lot of people have aired gripes about the writing and design of the guild quests, many of which I agree with. I do think the main quest is still fun for a "heroic fantasy pre-apocalyptic" backdrop to the otherwise humdrum, slice-of-life Adventurer Simulator that I treat this game as. But these days I tend to progress it up to the point where Oblivion Gates start spawning in the overworld, and then just close a few of those gates at my leisure. I find I have the most fun just trying to live my character's life for 10 or 15 levels, playing into whatever archetype or headcanon RP I've chosen for them, before taking a break or rerolling a different archetype.

This game has a lot of flaws. But I haven't found many other games that scratch the same "Adventurer Simulator" immersive RP itch, and that's not entirely nostalgia talking since I still play this clunky-ass game 20 years later. It's regularly on sale for $10 or less, so if the slice-of-life adventuring sounds like fun to you, it's worth a try.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion® Game of the Year Edition (2009) is widely regarded as one of the most influential open-world RPGs of its time, and for good reason. Building on the ambition of Morrowind, Oblivion introduced a richly detailed fantasy world filled with expansive quests, memorable guild storylines, and a groundbreaking level of player freedom. The addition of the Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles expansions in the GOTY edition only deepened its appeal. As an interactive fantasy world, Oblivion is one of the best examples out there but as a game, it fails to live up to the early 80s classics it is obviously predicated upon (Ultima, Might and Magic...). Especially when [url=https://www.wabbajack.org/#/modlists/info?machineURL=bevilex]modded[/url], the scenery can be breathtaking and hold up to any of its 2020 counterparts but the UI is clunky, the combat beyond barebones, dungeons are seldom memorable, NPCs are merely gateways to the simplest of RPG quests you'll see anywhere...

One might almost think that Oblivion would be better off not as an "epic action adventure" but instead as an exploration puzzle game where you need to travel around the fantastic, beautiful world to put together pieces of the grandest of puzzles by collecting knowledge and artifacts from every corner of Cyrodill... or perhaps a survival game like many Skyrim mods strive for. The combat, quests, magic system, skill system, etc. are more in the way than a core part of what makes the game alluring.

If you do play, get it on sale only and make sure you set yourself up to a challenge - things like "no save except for when resting" or "no loot except for stealing or pickpocketing". Otherwise, you'll find no challenge here except as a very casual player or young child starting their gaming adventures.

If Morrowind and many of the mentioned older games suffered from the exact same problems Oblivion does (despite it being a much more modern title), at least they made up for those flaws with actual gameplay challenges, ambitious dialogue systems, simulationist worlds, unique locations and characters or actually epic plot and quests... meanwhile, Oblivion is all icing and no cake. A great walking simulator for those that long to immerse themselves in fantasy but a pitiful attempt at the "game" portion of "video game".

Alt+tab, Windows key, ctrl+shift+escape were all disabled while the game ran. I spent at least a couple hours trying to get borderless windowed mode working just so I could use a second screen while playing the game, but nothing worked to get me out of the game except ctrl+alt+del to force open task manager, and that worked as a roundabout alt+tab, but crashed the game every time. Maybe my PC just wasn’t compatible, but with newer systems moving further from legacy support, these issues will likely become even worse for future players.

Oblivion’s narrative still impresses. Its worldbuilding and quest design hold their weight even today. But from a gameplay standpoint, the original version struggles under the weight of outdated mechanics, clunky UI, and pacing issues that can frustrate new players. I would probably recommend this if I had played 10+ years ago and gained some fond memories of my experiences despite the outdated mechanics it had even then. If you're coming in fresh, I’d recommend trying the remastered version instead. It likely offers a more accessible experience while preserving the story’s strengths.

The main story is fairly good, short, but good. The leveling system is simple yet adds a lot to how you want to play. The other great positive is the resolution options including ultra-wide support and a plethora of display and graphical options to make this game look less 2006 and more like 2010, meaning, it isn't nearly as bad as playing it on the consoles that it originally came out on. 

Now to get to the bad portions. The combat is boring and the constant staggering becomes increasingly frustrating as it seems to never get better as you level. Speaking of leveling, the biggest gripe that many have already stated, the more you level, the more you're punished in terms of the difficulty of your foes so no amount of levels will make you feel powerful leaving you unsatisfied as it seems your character never quite feels like a high-level character or a true "Hero of Kvatch". Also, while the faction quests can be interesting, the factions themselves give me no real desire to learn about anything or anyone. It just feels like a "go here, do this, repeat, until the game is over" type of quest-lines.

Overall, it gets a 6/10. I would give it a 5 for a full "meh" experience, but it does at minimum have more Elder Scrolls lore and meme-worthy content.

My previous review was written for this version of the game, where I didn't interact with any of the mechanics of this game, or even explored this game beyond a surface level.
But I'm now writing this review, having not only played Oblivion (remastered) but also Morrowind right before Oblivion. Given that we're talking about the original version of Oblivion and not the Remaster, I'll not be concentrating on the enhancements made to the game in the remaster. I'll instead be talking about what this game is at its core, and how it's not worth playing.

The elder scrolls games are a series of games that started as dungeon crawlers, that evolved into an open world RPG, with an emphasis on dungeon crawling. Unfortunately, Oblivion is a dungeon crawling game with bad dungeons. Why? Well, not only are there no rewards to completing dungeons, there are barely any stories. Most of the dungeons are copy pastes of one another, and the loot is maybe a few coins and some other pointless rubbish. Unlike both the predecessor Morrowind, and the successor Skyrim, this game gives you no reason to just go in some direction and just randomly clear out dungeons. There's literally no incentive to do so, because there are no rewards. In Morrowind you could end up with powerful enchantented weapons, or end up at some extraordinarily weird places the likes of which you'd not seen before. There was a sense of mystery and adventure to going somewhere in Morrowind. And there were certain places, where you were just not meant to go. Like a kwama farm. In Skyrim, going off in a random direction and enterring a new dungeon meant that not only could you get some great rewards, but you may also encounter new characters or incredible stories that made exploration interesting. In Oblivion, you should only venture out into a dungeon if you have been instructed to do so by a quest that you received in one of the cities. Otherwise it's pointless.

Now lets talk about the cities, and how outside the main imperial city, none of them have any character whatsoever. Sure they look different, but none of them have any personality. There's skingrad with a vampire count, but that's it. Him being a vampire doesn't affect anything. As a character he doesn't do anything. And honestly there's nothing in any of the cities that makes them memorable. In Skyrim every single main city had a story, that made those places memorable because those stories were so central to the identity of those cities. Be it Markarth and the forsworn, or be it Whiterun and the rivalry between Gray-Manes and the Battle-Borns. In Morrowind, there's well just all the intricate politics of the houses that makes everything so memorable.Not to mention, the otherworldly achitecture. Oblivion's cities lack depth of character and are generic and completely unmemorable.

The guilds are a downgrade from Morrowind too. In Morrowind, you couldn't just become the top guy in any guild by just doing all the quests. You also had to improve your stats to match the specifications required to become the top guy in any guild. And most of the guild tasks, were actual menial tasks conducted by a guild ( depending on the guiid)
Here in Oblivion we have a de-evolution of guilds. No more skill checks, missions are just, go here do this.And then you become the top guy in the faction. Worst is that even the guilds are not well written. The mages guild has a terrible main story, and is just awful. The fighters guild had a chance to deliver an emotional impact, when the guild leader's last son also dies. But we don't get to see any of the grief from the guild leader who lost her son. TL;DR: I've played Oblivion quite a lot before Steam, and it's an okay game when modded, but I just don't see much reason playing it these days. Definitely, if someone wants to play Oblivion, there are worse ways to spend your time, but there are also better, IMO. So this is mostly a neutral, slightly negative review.

Longer story: I was a big fan of Morrowind and got Oblivion when it came out. Oblivion is definitely very different to Morrowind. Graphics looked great at the time. Skill system is simplified. There are definitely good things. I love the negotiation system in Oblivion, where you can see the NPC's face react.

The main thing that absolutely killed Oblivion for me was the level scaling. It's not fun. Monsters scale with player level, and unless you optimize and min-max everything, your character actually gets weaker as you progress. Even areas that were safe before get harder. So you're penalized for doing side quests. The first time I played Oblivion, I did as many side quests as possible, but ended up getting stuck because I just couldn't kill any of the enemies anymore, it was too slow. Later when Game of the Year Edition was out I tried again and played only the main quest, ignoring side quests. It was much easier. If you focus on the main quest, it's a very easy game. Not really worth it, because I found the main story really nonsense, as it usually is in Elder Scrolls. They're not really focusing on the main quest, it's all about the side quests. So if you really want to play it properly and do side quests, you really need to optimize the skills you raise. It's actually more optimal to choose skills that you don't use often as your main skills, so you can control when you level up. Then you end up using out of character skills when you want to level up. Or you just don't level up. This goes completely against how I see role playing.

There are of course ways to fix this with mods, but I'm too old to bother looking up mods and installing them in a certain order just to play a game. There's no point in my opinion. Skyrim is just as good IMO, and it works without modding. I see Skyrim as Oblivion v2.0, and while not perfect, I enjoyed it more.

I also don't like the list-based inventory system, which makes it difficult to sort out the equipment and see what you have.

TES IV: Oblivion was a technical leap forward in game engines and AI, and was, in retrospect, a necessary stepping-stone on the way to landmark titles like Fallout: New Vegas and Skyrim. On its own, however, it was a remarkably half-baked experience, and heralded a new age of mediocre, made-for-console RPGs with only as much depth as could be neatly managed by an Xbox controller.

Of its myriad technical innovations, Oblivion's most daring by far was its Radiant AI, which was at the time the most fully realized NPC AI ever seen in an RPG. It promised to breathe life into the game world by simulating NPC behavior, but it wasn't enough on its own. In fact, the game's chief mistake was its broad overreliance on that system to generate interactions, a mistake compounded by the failure of its designers to transition from writing for stationary placeholder NPCs to writing for the more dynamic, realistic characters which Radiant allowed.

Oblivion's NPCs were more lifelike than those of the previous games, to be sure, but only just enough to get our brains to judge them by criteria we’d apparently given their more cartoonish predecessors a pass on. Behavior that had seemed fine for the largely static characters of Morrowind (like making frank declarations of name and occupation, apropos of nothing, when addressed by a complete stranger) now seemed glaringly fake, now that animations and models were realistic enough to make players expect NPCs to act like actual people. It certainly didn't help that the game was fully voiced, but was only read by a grand total of perhaps 5 voice actors.

And it was clear that, as revolutionary an idea as Radiant might have been, the game's designers hadn't quite figured out how to best work with it. NPC transitions between behaviors and dialogue were infamously abrupt and without respect to context, resulting in hilariously jarring or inappropriate interactions only made worse by jerky animations and disruptive camera handling.

TES IV did no better on the merits of its story, either, which proved to be as tepid and forgettable as those of the first two games. In the Oblivion crisis and the Hero of Kvatch, the developers had found the wrong answer to the question “how do we make randomly generated quests as interesting as the main plot?” (The right answer is you should hope you can't.) The protagonist earns his title within the first hour of play, and is destined thereafter to never achieve anything more noteworthy, serving only as glorified sidekick to the true hero, a Septim bastard. In my headcanon, you don't actually escape from Oblivion the first time you enter it, and the rest of the game is illusory: a boring, private hell full of gibbering non player idiots, made just for you by Mehrunes Dagon.

Bland, too, was the visual backdrop of the game, which closely aped those of contemporaneous blockbuster movies: Cyrodiil was an uninspired clone of Peter Jackson’s Gondor, while the motif of the Deadlands, in all its red and black tackiness, seems to have been cribbed from the Star Wars prequels. To add insult to injury, the game's most prominent 3D assets - characters and weapons - were needlessly ugly even by 2006's standards. As in Morrowind, however, the music was actually very good and, in my opinion, may have been the main reason why Oblivion was so widely well received on release.

I've revisited Oblivion occasionally over the last 15 years and have found very little to recommend it. The best thing I can think to say of it was that it served as a staging area for better things which have come since then, both from Bethesda and the community. Apart from selling a ton of copies, it failed to accomplish what it had set out to do (simulate a believable world), but would see its foresight and technical investments largely vindicated by its sequel, TESV.

However, by the time that I started leveling up from going on multiple quests was when I discovered the largest issue with Oblivion: its level scaling. The level scaling of every creature made this game near unplayable for me, because half of the gameplay loop is playing ring-around-the-rosy with the difficulty slider. That, combined with the issue of the ugly art style caused me to quit playing this game after only 11 hours. However, it is not all bad. The NPC behavior is quite fluid for its time, and can be quite funny at times. The addition of the Adoring Fan is also quite welcome, and made the whole experience MUCH better. Plus, many of the side quests were quite goofy and fun. Overall, I would not suggest playing Oblivion unless you have nostalgia for the game. Lifeless and bland open world with nothing but computer generated slop in between the major cities. Almost every single area in the game is the same forest biome. Sure, there are dungeons here and there, mostly caves and ayleid ruins. The thing is, they are all the exact same. I promise you won't ever see a dungeon that's different from the other's. I've seen people praise this game for it's world, but there really isn't anything interesting in it. It also feels boring as hell. There are no quests to be randomly found out there in the world, all of them are given to you by talking to NPCs in the cities. The loot you can find in dungeons is randomly generated, and you won't find any unique items from exploring. There is simply no incentive to explore, and no reward for doing so. 

There's no point in exploring, just to where your quest marker points. In my first few hours I tried not to use fast travel, but walking around the open world is just not fun (and there's no point in doing so). This is not an exploration game, the world itself is just a backdrop, this game's only worthwhile content are the quests. I have heard much praise for Oblivion's quests, both the main quest, the factions questlines and the random NPC ones. To be honest, I can't criticise these, because I haven't finished any of the faction's questlines, nor the main quest. From what I've played so far, though, there where some interesting quests, sure, like the one in which you go into a painted world, or the one with the paranoic dude in Skingrad. But the thing is, these quest have good premises and all that, but in terms of how they play out in the gameplay, they are not that great. Yeah there are interesting quests, but in the end they are all fetch quests, some with some killing in the middle. 

But I can accept that. I honestly would love to keep playing the game and play through every single questline to see if they get as interesting as people say they do. However, this game's gameplay and leveling suck ass. It's not fun to play when the enemies become unkillable damage sponges that can tank all of your attacks for 10 minutes. I'm not talking about a boss or anything, no, just a simple golbin or mountain lion. Every single enemy levels up with you, which means that you won't feel any sense of progression. If anything, you will feel weaker at higher levels than at lvl 1. If you don't use an optimal build from some guide, the game will feel like shit. The combat is already worse than in Skyrim, but this makes it unplayable. 

The Oblivion Gates themselves are also the same copypasted dungeon dozens of times, The NPCs' faces are nightmare fuel, and the AI is terrible. The cities are actually pretty good. They are bigger than Skyrim's. However, they do all look kinda the same, whereas Skyrim's cities all felt unique. Skyrim also had decent towns and villages here and there, this game does not. Also, I've encountered several quest-breaking bugs that made me wanna throw my PC out the window. I also didn't like the Imperial City, I think it's one of the worse-looking cities in the game, actually. There is also no roleplaying mechanics. You can join every single faction, your decisions don't seem to matter. Also the dialogue sucks.

All in all, my opinion of this game is pretty negative. While I played, I constantly went from bored to frustrated. But I did have some good moments and fun here and there. I just feel like my fun was ruined by the horrid game design and art direction. I started in this game thinking it would blow me away, but instead it left me dissapointed. I expect much more from the open world of the Imperial Province, but it turned out to be a soulless computer generated world with nothing to see but the same green forests and generic dungeons. 

I believe most people that recommend the game are biased by nostialgia. I don't think it's a fun game, and the main story, quests and dialogue (let's not even talk about the roleplaying aspect of the game) are just way worse than in real rpg's lilke Pathfinder or Baldur's Gate games. The only thing is has going for it is the amazing Elder Scrolls Lore.

I might give it another try with mods sometime in the future, but as a vanilla experience this game is horrible.

[h1]From the most unbiased perspective I can muster, this is objectively the worst game in the franchise.[/h1] 

[b]This may be hard to hear, especially since the common opinion on this game is a positive one, But this is why.[/b]

Now, Oblivion is an undeniable classic which I used to love, and it does a lot of things right. First off, the music, like all Elder Scrolls games, is absolutely fire. This game competes with Morrowind has having my favorite take on the Elder Scrolls theme. It's theme is energetic, and majestic, and more "fancy" when compared to Skyrim's and Morrowind's more gritty takes on it. Another thing is that Shivering Isles has possibly my favorite questline in an RPG ever. Sheogorath is absolutely represented at his best in this one. The player homes are fun and cool, and the dungeons and caves are actually incredibly diverse compared to other titles. The guild quests are also quite good, and despite having a pathetic main quest, some of the objectives in the story are really fun. Some of the dialogue is excellent too, and a solid bunch of the characters in this game are incredibly interesting. That's where the good ends.

TES IV Oblivion is far from a nice looking game, with muddy textures, low detail models, and frankly disgusting characters. The colors, while bright and somewhat nice looking in the overworld, look terrible indoors and in caves/dungeons. This is utterly disappointing when you compare it to the completely stylized nature of Morrowind, or the more realistic looking nature of Skyrim.

Despite being one of the more populated and vast countries in Tamriel (according to lore), This game is barren and empty. A perfect example of this is the Imperial City. In Elder Scrolls lore, The imperial city is massive and home to more than a million, including most of the imperial elites on the continent, as well as folk of other races working on the streets. In oblivion, despite being the biggest city in the game and having multiple districts and map loads, [b]The imperial city feels quite miniature and leaves out an unforgivable amount of content, especially when compared to Mournhold from Morrowind's DLC Tribunal.[/b] This is a pattern across every city in any elder scrolls game (it sadly has to be so due to technology limitations), however this particular instance is absolutely worst case scenario. It is very difficult to imagine a worse interpretation of the only in-game instance of the most important city in Tamriel. 

The NPCs are unbearably bad. Despite being hyped back in the day as being groundbreaking and game changing, [b]The NPCs in oblivion are either fundamentally unfinished, or coded by literal monkeys.[/b] Their path detection consistently leads them to get stuck on each other as wells as in game objects. In combat, its very possible (especially in dungeons) for them to become permenently stuck and immobile, allowing for cheese kills (which is especially infuriating when its a boss or challenging quest enemy). As said before, They're also all disgusting and unappealing to look at. There is not a single character that looks good in this game, and no possible way to make your character look even remotely decent without mods. There's also a lack of diversity in faces and clothing. There's a reoccurring issue in Elder Scrolls games, in which, most characters seem all commonly wear only 1 of 10 or so "clothes" type outfits.. But in oblivion, it feels like there's 4. There's also a large fundamentally flawed issue with the NPC leveling that makes the game progressively harder as you level up until you get to a point where all enemies are god tier compared to yourself, even after you beat it and become a legend, but its too much to explain in this petty steam review, So if learning more about this is appealing to you, I highly recommend watching EphiTV's shockingly short video on the subject, titled [url=https://youtu.be/NNlILuseQJw] "Why Oblivion's leveling system is so broken". [/url] 

The leveling and RPG mechanics are commonly credited as being superior to Skyrim's, and while I agree with that, I wouldn't say they its by much at all. Bethesda completely gutted half of the interesting mechanics from Morrowind. Skyrim's skill system is bad, and un-detailed, however Skyrim itself as a game is very playable and enjoyable, despite being flawed in its own ways, [b]which is not something that can be said about this one.[/b]

The best thing about Bethesda games are the mod support, and ability to mod the game into whatever type of RPG you would like to play. I dislike Skyrim's leveling system and lack of true interaction with NPCs, however, I use mods that make literally every sapient non enemy NPC interactable with more dialogue options as well as mods that completely change the skill system. While there are mods for that for oblivion (they aren't super great), The mod support is practically non existent to half the player base, including me, because of a few fundamental issues that make loading custom files with Oblivion impossible. If you have certain hardware, or if your pc has one of the millions of small quirks that the game doesn't like, kiss mod support goodbye. This is my fourth PC I've installed oblivion on, and even with the help of an actual Oblivion modder in a discord call, I have never once been able to play this game beyond one instance where the game didn't crash on launch. I made it to the starting area, and instantly realized that half of the games textures had been deleted, including the ones on characters. The only mod I had installed when this happened was a mod that changes the glass weaponry to a Skyrim blue instead of green. A further problem with the mod support is that there are 3 or 4 types of community mod installation methods, and each method is incompatible with another method. Most mods are only compatible with being installed through one of these 4 methods. This effectively cuts the amount of mods you'll ever be able to use to a fourth of the mods on nexus, it all just depends on what method you use. 

[b] Overall, This game is absolutely terrible, and I wouldn't even recommend buying it on sale. [/b] Just buy Morrowind or Skyrim. The quests in this one (excluding the entire knights of the nine and shivering isles dlc) are mediocre anyways. If someone were to rate Skyrim was a 5/10 game, in comparison to that, i would say Oblivion falls to a puny [b]3/10[/b]. This review hurt to make due to nostalgia, but Its a hard truth I had to face.

Personally, I feel that the game is a pretty meh experience. About a 5-6/10 for me (not bad based on how I rate things, but not really good either). A 5 for me is a game that is meh, but I'm bored and have to force myself to keep playing it. 

I saw all of the positive reviews, and I can see how people would adore it back in the day, but after playing, I didn't have the same experience. I was really hyped to give it a try, and I may have set the bar a little too high. I just got away from playing Skyrim (kinda a boring game for me as well, but that's its own story) and was looking for more of an RPG experience. I heard that in Oblivion, the story is amazing, quests are great, the world is cool, and there is actually color other than grey/brown (big point for me coming from Skyrim). I mean come on, who wouldn't expect a great game with a 95% positive rating with around eighteen thousand reviews. Also, it was like $6... why not give it a shot. 

I promise, I tried. I really did, but man, maybe I'm just an old jaded gamer (not that old, I'm in my 20s)  with no time anymore, but this was a boring experience after about five hours. Credit where credit is due. I got to make a class. That was really cool, and the abilities I chose affected how I played. Also, I liked the skills more than in Skyrim. You really had a chance to make your own character, which I can say is what I came for, but that wasn't enough in the end.

The story.... kind of an oof. If you talk to someone, they're going to say it's so much bigger than Skyrim. "Instead of dragons, you get to fight the forces of hell, and a demon god dude." The problem is, it's really slow and doesn't feel as grand as people make it sound. There's a lot of, "go here, kill the baddies, get the item, and come back." And y'all, that's just how I see it. I'm sure (15,000 plus people) really enjoyed the experience and really were engaged in the story. I was not. I never felt the desire to care about anything in the story. Let's be clear, I didn't finish it (boo shame on me, I know), but I don't want to finish it. I know what happens, so that's my defense, but still. In my opinion, if a game's story is not interesting enough/engaging enough for me to care, I shouldn't have to force myself to care. 

The characters don't bring much. Now, all the game characters are somewhat dynamic and react to things, which is pretty cool in its own right, but that's not going to make a game great. It's just a cool feature that adds to the overall experience, but if the overall experience is meh... cool features will make it meh+ I guess. I never cared about a single person I met. Sure they had some personality, which is more than a lot of games can say, but it doesn't change the fact that I don't care about them. No single character made an impression on me and their writing didn't cut it.

So finally, I guess I should talk about the gameplay. It exists.. It's a clunkier version of Skyrim, being the older game and all. Aesthetically, it looked way better, but it doesn't change the fact that it's old. If coming from Skyrim like me, you'll have to get over some QoL stuff, but honestly, that's no big deal. Being able to cast spells while wielding two weapons was really cool. Having skills like acrobatics was fun. Like I said though... it's clunky Skyrim. The clunk has a nice charm to it, but I don't like the repetitive nature of everything. It's pretty boring after fighting a couple hundred enemies. Also, I'm gonna tell you straight. Oblivion gates are not that cool after the first one. I promise.

So, like I said earlier, 5-6/10 for me. You know, if you are interested in the game and what it has to offer, I'd say give it a shot. I wouldn't recommend it if you asked me, but I'm not gonna stop you. Read the other reviews on here, but try to filter out the nostalgia people. Not that having fond memories of a game is a bad thing, but I caution against listening to someone who only played the game years ago as it will usually only be good things. I have those games too (Conflict Desert Storm or Banjo Tooie), but even the best of games have their flaws. You need to see both side of the coin. Seeing a review: "10/10 you can be Jesus and walk on water" might not be the best example of the game (but it is pretty fun playing Jesus). So I'll leave it up to you. I've said my piece and it's up to you to decide. It's old, but might be gold. Give it a shot if you are interested.

As a longtime fan of The Elder Scrolls series, Oblivion left me disappointed. Instead of building on what made the series great, it followed a generic RPG formula. Bethesda promised a vast world, but the game felt shallow with a bland main quest and recycled content. Side quests quickly became repetitive, lacking depth.

The Radiant AI and dynamic world were gimmicks with little impact on gameplay. The leveling system forced players into constrained builds, limiting creativity. The Oblivion Gates became tiresome, highlighting stretched content.

The game tried to appeal to a modern audience, but it alienated fans by dumbing down mechanics and lore. The visuals and sound were impressive, but couldn't replace the loss of the series' magic. Combat felt clunky and outdated.

The first paid DLC for horse skins felt like a cash grab, undermining the idea of a rich world. Ultimately, Oblivion missed the mark, trying to appeal to everyone while losing its soul. The paid DLCs only reinforced the feeling of a game more focused on monetization than quality.

As an avid fan of The Elder Scrolls series, I decided to revisit The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion despite its dated graphics. While the game may not hold up well in terms of visuals compared to modern titles, its charm lies in its immersive world and captivating gameplay.

One aspect that disappointed me was the limited and buggy controller support. To fully enjoy the game, I had to use both the keyboard and controller simultaneously since some game mechanics weren't compatible with the controller. This inconvenience made me question the usefulness of using a controller with the game. If you're a fan of using controllers, you might find this aspect frustrating.

However, for die-hard fans of The Elder Scrolls franchise, revisiting Oblivion can be a rewarding experience. The game's vast open world, rich lore, and engaging quests still manage to captivate players even after all these years. Exploring the detailed landscapes, encountering unique characters, and embarking on epic adventures are still as thrilling as ever.

One of the game's redeeming qualities is the extensive modding community that has flourished over the years. The NexusMods platform offers a plethora of free mods that can enhance and customize your Oblivion experience. With the user-friendly Vortex mod manager, even those with limited technical knowledge can easily install mods. This allows players to tailor the game to their preferences and breathe new life into the aging graphics and gameplay mechanics.

Overall, if you're an Elder Scrolls fan, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is worth a replay. Despite its outdated graphics and limited controller support, the game's immersive world and captivating gameplay make it a worthwhile experience. The availability of free mods further extends its longevity, allowing players to customize their adventures and add fresh content to the game.
