[code]While The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion might still be of interest for Elder Scrolls fans, it did not age well enough that I’d recommend it as an entry point to the franchise for anyone else[/code]

A necessary info before I go on with the review itself: My playthrough of [i]Oblivion[/i] was completely mod-free. I’m reviewing the game as-is, without any additions made by the community.

Considering the massive popularity of its sequel, [i]Skyrim[/i], I always wondered why [i]Oblivion[/i] seemed to receive way less attention these days. Considering the two seemed to share quite a few mechanics, it stroked me as odd. However, once I was finished with my playthrough of the [i]Oblivion[/i] main quest as well as the Shivering Isles expansion, I got my answer: The two aren’t just as similar as I thought to be. But more importantly, one thing became clear: Since its original release in 2006, the passing years haven’t been kind to [i]Oblivion[/i]. As a result, as unfortunate as it is, [i]Oblivion[/i] feels extremely dated and clunky a lot of the time.

Let’s start with the basics: As a prisoner stuck inside a cell, you’re suddenly granted an unexpected escape. After a few basic tutorials for movement and combat, you’re dropped into the world of Cyrodiil – with a mission to save the entire place from a world-ending threat of course. Thanks to the various DLCs included in the GOTY edition, you’ll also receive quite a lot of quests, like visiting a new home or getting armor for your horse, while still escaping the prison. [i]“According to a mysterious message that's been delivered to me, I've inherited an underground lair called Deepscorn Hollow from a long-lost relative“[/i] – who exactly delivered this note to me while I’m escaping through the sewers?

Once out of prison and entering the overworld of Cyrodiil, you’ll be greeted with a vast landmass, filled with the usual cities, dungeons, ruins and more. However, as you’ll quickly discover, despite all these points of interest, Cyrodiil turns out to be quite a lonely place. Outside of the livelier settlements, there’s just a lot of empty space with an occasional bear or bandit to meet. It doesn’t help that many parts of the world look the same. The various planes of Oblivion I visited as part of the main quest, for example, consist of just the few same assets that get moved around a bit for each Oblivion Gate. Same goes for a lot of the dungeons or caves. As I didn’t want to explore the same caves over and over again, I made the decision to skip exploring them and focus on the main quest instead.

The main quest of [i]Oblivion[/i] is pretty much a predictable affair and doesn’t offer anything you haven’t seen in other fantasy works already. It quickly devolves into the usual assignment list of things to do in order to save the world - without any huge surprises, memorable deeds to accomplish or stunning places to visit. That said, for Elder Scrolls fans, [i]Oblivion[/i] offers a lot of lore to involve yourself in, be it through books, dialogues or more.

Throughout the main quest, of course, there’s a lot of fighting (against a very limited arrangement of enemy types) to be done. For this game, I decided to build a melee-heavy character, focusing on blades, sometimes shields and heavy armor. Turns out that leads to a gameplay loop of just wieldy swinging around a sword via left click to slowly chip away at an enemy’s health bar. As it hard to tell how long your (or the enemy’s) effective strike range actually is, moving in and out for strikes is not an option. Blocking turned out to be somewhat unreliable as well and some enemies also got the nasty habits of stunlocking you through multiple consecutive attacks. This can prove especially deadly if your character gets stuck in the level geometry because of it.

Presented with the option of spamming left click to attack and using the occasional health potion/restoration spell to slowly fight through enemy hordes (or well, hordes of the same few enemy types), I clung to the hope of a good gear progression that maybe would make fights less annoying. That didn’t really happen during my main story-focused playthrough though: All the (better) weapons or armor I saw were in the same attack/defense number range. Looking at the [i]Oblivion[/i] wiki pages, there do seem to be way more (effective) weapons in the game - but at least during the main quests I didn’t encounter them.

 What I did encounter way more often than I wanted to, though, were technical problems. Some of them might be helpful, it’s really easy to get enemies or even bosses stuck in various objects – trivializing many fights. It’s less helpful when this happens to quest NPCs though. Other bugs include items disappearing through the ground when dropped by enemies, saves getting corrupted or even game crashes. The latter happened annoyingly often, which makes the quick-save button probably one of my most used buttons during my playthrough. There are a lot of unofficial patches for the game though, so probably consider installing one if you still want to pick [i]Oblivion[/i] up.

After finishing the underwhelming and short main quest of [i]Oblivion[/i], I gave the – surprisingly lengthy – Shivering Isles expansion a try. While it does start off more promising by offering a more unique setting, taking place in the realm of a mad prince, it sadly didn’t really stay that way. It also quickly devolves into a predictable “go here, do that for me” assignment list in a mostly lifeless domain – that’s shockingly normal looking for a supposed twisted place of madness. It’s also disappointing how the gameplay remains completely unchanged in this expansion. However, if you liked the base game of [i]Oblivion[/i], you’re probably going to have a good time with this expansion as well.

While we’re on the topic of madness, there’s one last thing I want to give a shout-out to: The horrible UI and menu design. This is probably one of the aspects where the age of [i]Oblivion[/i] shows the most, turning even simple tasks like quickly changing your armor into a tedious undertaking. If you can find any mod out there that’s improving this UI experience, install it without any doubt, there’s nothing to be lost.

Concluding, I can’t say that my revisit of [i]Oblivion[/i] after playing it back in 2008 didn’t turn out to be a letdown for me. I had a considerably worse time than I expected. As such, I can’t really recommend [i]Oblivion[/i] to anyone who isn’t already thinking about playing the game because they’re a fan of the franchise. If you are, go look for some mods patching up the experience and as long as you’re not expecting to be [i]Skyrim 2[/i], you’re probably good to go. If you aren’t, if you want to take a look at the franchise, check out [i]Skyrim[/i] instead – it’s popular for a reason.

Sandwiched between one of the most effective worldbuilding exercises in Morrowind and one of the greatest dungeon-delving exploration playgrounds in Skyrim, Oblivion's role as the bridge is defined by the weaknesses of the former and the weaknesses of the latter all nicely squished together in one dreadful experience. Problems misinterpreted and haphazardly fixed from Morrowind, most notably a complete overhaul of leveling and progression, are a continuous headache from the beginning to the end. Story and writing are a significant, open gash on the flank of the game, with little to no depth or complexity in character motivations or personality and scant evidence of prose﻿ at any point. Voice acting ranges from passable (with fabled actors somehow being wasted on monotonous deliveries and boring dialogue) to utterly abysmal (when so many of the actors are the same, the voices really do begin to mush together, making immemorable characters even more invisible). Combat is just.. terrible. Staggers pausing actions at nearly every other swing, overabundant enemies, and a frustrating synchronization of damage-type-locked ghosts and quickly-draining enchanted weapons makes for dull at best, repulsive at worst fighting. Most severe of the woes are an unintuitive, broken, and disbalanced leveling system that functionally lets the player level "down", by not making it clear how badly you can kneecap yourself if you're not taking +5 attribute boosts when sleeping. This is the only game I have played in the last decade that I had to turn the difficulty down in to progress - enemies scaled beyond weapons that I picked up from them, with turbo-inflated health pools, could not be beaten without careful wait-regain scumming. There are positives, like exceptionally creative quest design, good music, and a very freeing magic and enchanting system, but these are difficult to appreciate in the face of everything else. Oblivion struggles to be worth the time it can take up, and though it's from a legendary line of games, it's a legend I'd prefer put to rest.

Based on the timing and context of their recent social media actions, Bethesda Softworks appears to be protecting developers who have publicly endorsed and celebrated the recent assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. In a now-deleted tweet from their official X account, the company deflected criticism of these employees' conduct by sharing a clip from Indiana Jones and the Great Circle that indirectly labeled concerned users (and, as interpreted by many on X, potentially Kirk himself) as 'fascists.' Given this apparent defense of staff who revel in the murder of an innocent man, I cannot in good conscience purchase or recommend any titles from the publisher.

Regardless of whether Bethesda promptly terminates the offending employees, dismisses the responsible social media manager, and issues a formal apology, such actions would not change my review of this specific title, as it is, in my opinion, the weakest in the series. While the side quests are the strongest out of any Elder Scrolls entry, most other aspect falls short in some respect. The most frustrating part of attempting to play this game is the fundamentally broken enemy HP and damage scaling. This [i]discourages[/i] leveling up, forcing you to select from a pool of very few major skills during character creation if you want to minmax your training at your own rate, capitalizing on attribute bonuses so that enemies don't demolish you at level 16 or so. This all culminates in a fundamentally miserable experience if your character specializes in combat but not optimized. As if this weren't enough, enemy detection radii are so massive that, when traversing Cyrodiil, you'll often hear combat music long before you notice or can even see what's pursuing you. What is particularly unsatisfying is how the magic system is more restrictive than Morrowind's but less streamlined than Skyrim's. Stealth is also much more difficult than in other entries without chameleon effects. On the whole, this makes most non-custom classes a chore to play.

The physics engine, while undoubtedly impressive for the time, has not aged perfectly, with most objects being less massive (easier to move) than they appear. Additionally, the gutted version of Radiant AI makes NPC interactions often nonsensical in the environmental context. Funny or charming moments arising from both these issues only do so much to curtail the immersion they destroy.

The NPC voice acting is disjointed, as certain NPCs are coded with both character/class specific voice lines in addition to generic, racial ones. For example, the male Imperial beggar sometimes sounds like a downtrodden tramp; at other times, he sounds like an Imperial Watchman depending on which dialogue option you select. This is more of a personal preference, but I disliked how the Nords shared voice actors with the Orcs.

The main storyline is weak, worse than Skyrim's. It is very straightforward without many unexpected twists. The one final twist is somewhat impactful in the context of the greater lore, if you care about that, at minimum laying the foundation for the next game: [spoiler]Emperor Martin Septim sacrifices himself by destroying the Amulet of Kings and transforming into Akatosh's Avatar to banish Mehrunes Dagon back to the Deadlands before turning to stone, stopping the Oblivion Crisis. This lays the groundwork to explain why a Mede sits on the throne after the Septim bloodline ended and why the Empire is weak enough to struggle to halt the Skyrim Civil War.[/spoiler] Aside from that singular highlight, the story is a series of predictable plot points interspersed with fetch quests, escort quests, lengthy dungeon crawls, and brief forays into Oblivion.

Aside from the quests at large, one other positive point I'll give it is how wonderfully crafted the Shivering Isles expansion is as a whole. The environments are beautiful, the storyline is riveting in the context of the Elder Scrolls lore, the quests are somehow even better than in the base game as they offer more intriguing choices, and the characters are unforgettable. It would almost be an inversion of the base game if not for the fact that level scaling still applies.

On modern hardware, the game is noticeably unstable. On my machine, I was constantly plagued with crashes. I failed to pinpoint an underlying cause. If you plan to play this (assuming you already own it, since I don't recommend you buy it now), maybe the [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/oblivion/mods/5296]Unofficial Oblivion Patch[/url] will provide you with a smoother experience than I had.

For the reasons outlined above, I feel compelled neither to buy the Remaster nor any other Bethesda product ever again.

Step through and you enter a hellish, spike-ridden landscape, strewn about with corpses and the occasional strange plant that will mess you up if you get too close. Of course, you soon come to learn that Oblivion Gates have no real effect on the world and that each one is basically the same as the last. I closed the minimum number of gates, and from the fourth one on pretty much just sprinted to the end to close it.

[i]Oblivion[/i] did get some things right though. For example, it added NPC scheduling (which had been done long before by games such as [i]Ultima VII[/i]). It just doesn't measure up to its predecessor, and is an overall dull experience.

I've played both this version and the new remastered version. My review is for the Re-Mastered version, but it's pretty much only improved on the original 2009 version in terms of gameplay and graphics. 

In short, I don't recommend Oblivion Remastered and especially not this version if you're not going in with nostalgia goggles. It's not a very good game: it's buggy, poorly balanced, incredibly janky, and the only thing really impressive about the Remaster is the visuals, which are actually pretty good and the biggest difference between the two versions. 

The best thing about this game is the sheer confidence of its earnest jankiness, which you have to respect at times. 

However, Skyrim in reality is better in almost every conceivable way. A great example of the sheer chasm of difference between Oblivion and Skyrim is vampirism. In Skyrim, being a vampire is a surprisingly in-depth experience that involves a cool vampire-form with numerous unique abilities, including a perk tree to expand on those abilities further. 

In Oblivion on the other hand, being a vampire is a miserable and incredibly annoying experience that gets forced on you the first time you fight against vampires, and which has almost no gameplay depth to it other than not being able to fast-travel during the day unless you can find someone to feed on (harder than it sounds). 

Heck, even though being a werewolf in Skyrim is fairly underwhelming, at least it has the option to be a werewolf at all (unlike Oblivion). Wait, never mind, I just double-checked for factual accuracy and apparently a perk tree was added to being a werewolf in the Dawnguard DLC for Skyrim, so it's actually more on par with playing a vampire than I thought (even if still not on the same level). 

Yet people try to pretend Oblivion is somehow more in-depth, and after the 24 hours of so playing Oblivion again and then going back to Skyrim to compare, I simply don't see almost any way in which this is true, beyond perhaps spell-crafting--except that was partially added in Skyrim: Special Edition as well, and spell-crafting is a pretty boring and broken feature, anyway. What else does Oblivion have over Skyrim? The awful persuasion mechanic that no one likes? Or perhaps the worst lockpicking system in the history of gaming as opposed to Skyrim's simple but much more enjoyable version? 

I could go on, but I don't have enough additional points to make since so many of the quests I tried to do in Oblivion simply kept bugging out on me. In short, stay away and play Skyrim instead. Or if you're looking for more isometric fantasy games, Age of Decadence, Baldur's Gate 3 and Divinity 2 are all great.

tl;dnr: It’s boring.
Oblivion is an RPG set in a standard fantasy (what an awful term). You are some nameless bloke who apparently is the only one who can stop the world from impending doom from the hellscape of Oblivion (the actual place, not the game, though saving the World from the game Oblivion is also a worthy and necessary cause).

First, the Gameplay. Building your character (Class, Race, Strength, etc) in Oblivion is a disastrous and unintuitive mess that really, REALLY wants to be interesting and cool. If you have any idea of making an optimized Oblivion character, purge that idea from your mind now. Making a good character requires manually tallying when your skills increase, or you risk gaining less power when you level up. Oblivion’s character creation is certainly complex, but lacks any real depth. But the gameplay isn’t always that bad. The combat is actually fairly good for a Single Player RPG, allowing you to actually mix spells, weapon tactics, positioning, and other factors in meaningful ways, due to all the buffs and boosts you can layer onto your character. Unfortunately, that means nothing, since the all enemies do the same thing: stand still and attack you. No interesting abilities, no unique movement patterns, nothing at all. 

Second, the Story. Like I mentioned earlier, the setting of Oblivion is boring and uninteresting, with nothing new. I think all games should ask some kind of question to the player. Spec Ops: The Line asks you if you feel like a hero. Fallout asks you about the relationship between Conflict and Technology. Oblivion asks you how long you can stare at a computer screen before you opt to drive a railroad spike through your brain. I actually have a low hour count for how large this game is, and that’s because I cannot force myself to play this game any further because it so impossibly boring. Oblivion does make an attempt: the stories aren’t “kill more bandits, then some more bandits”, or “deliver this letter for me”. But that’s always how the quests end: there’s no real intrigue or information: all relevant knowledge just falls in your lap if you sit through enough NPC dialogue, requiring no input on your part.

Third the Artwork and Sound. Oblivion has awful graphics, but I honestly don’t care about that as long as the artwork is good. To be perfectly fair, the artwork is OK. I can tell what everything is, and everything fits within the bland mush that is “Standard Fantasy”. The soundtrack is so impossibly mediocre that it is hard to comprehend. It does nothing that could possibly cause you to enjoy it. The voice acting is the nail in the coffin for this game. I would almost tell you to buy the game just to witness how awful the voice acting is, but I’m not a sadist.

So here’s the final verdict: Oblivion is boring. Impossible boring. In the game, Oblivion is a terrifying hellscape, but the game Oblivion is an endless purgatory. 
Rather than attach a dumb numerical score to games, I ask two questions: Is it Worth your time, and Is it Worth your Money?
Oblivion is not worth your time. It is a boring and drab experience, whose only saving grace is that it lacks the skinner box mechanics that suck you in that are omnipresent in triple A games today.
Obviously, if it is not worth your time, it is not worth your money. I cannot recommend this game.

"Oblivion is the best Elder Scrolls game"
Is what I keep hearing from fans of the game. And I want to believe them, I really do. I tried so hard to love this game, but anyone who says that Oblivion is a masterpiece is neglecting to mention it's flaws.

In my opinion there is nothing wrong with the actual gameplay. It is challenging but fair, and overall everything from weapons to armor is pretty balanced, and swordplay, archery, and magic all take some level of skill and are fun and engaging to use. Oblivion's biggest problem, and what really makes it a chore to play, is it's absolutely broken level-up system. If you're new to the game you'll likely make the mistake of choosing to play as the class that reflects your playstyle. (yes, you read that right) Oblivion's leveling system punishes you for choosing your main skills and using them because whenever you level a major skill it counts toward a level-up. You need to level 10 major skills to level-up, but the amount your stats increase as you level up is based off how many TOTAL skills you level up, even ones that aren't relevant to you. Making it mathematically impossible to have a decently-leveled character without doing some amount of grinding at each level. (god help you if you chose athletics or acrobatics as a major skill, you won't be able to run without screwing yourself with leveling. I am not joking)
The system is so broken that whenever I play it, it makes me feel like I have to limit my actions and modify my playstyle just to not mess up leveling. (This is the kind of game where your level/stats matter for everything, so you need to have good stats or your character will be useless). The only remedy for this is to either play on easy mode or just avoid leveling up the entire game. It ruins any feeling of progression the game has. I shouldn't HAVE to do any of that to avoid the atrocious leveling system. I Should be able to just play the game as the class I want to play as. (online guides actually reccomend that to play your character effectively, you should choose the opposite class of what you want to play as. Wanna play as a spellcaster? Better choose a warrior class. Wanna be a sneaky rouge? you're better off picking a barbarian. Want to play an archer? just play a sorcerer and pick up a bow. You'll level-up more efficiently than you would picking the actual archer class.)

I'm so sick of not being able to do simple things my character should be able to do like running, jumping, attacking, and casting spells just because I feel like: "whoops, I've cast too many Destruction spells this level. I know I'm a wizard but I'd better put on some heavy armor and a shield and stand around letting myself get hit on purpose so my health won't be atrocious at later levels." It ruins any form of immersion. In my current playthrough the game doesn't even count the skills I've gained, so no matter how efficiently I grind I can never get an optimized level-up. I don't know if this is a bug, but half the time the game doesn't even follow it's own ridiculous rules.

Beyond that, all other problems with the game are minor. There are a few glitches, and depending on your system the game might be buggy, but most of that can be fixed by updating your drivers, as it's an older game. The dialouge between NPC's is absolutely iconic as meme-material, even if it's really robotic and unnatural.

Beyond that the gameplay is stellar and the story is amazing. Or so I've been told. I haven't been able to play past the first few missions because the grinding get so tedious it makes the rest of the game unfun. 
I wish I could say I loved this game. I tried my best to immerse myself, but any immersion is almost immediately quelled by the worst leveling system ever implimented. It honestly breaks my heart to have to leave a negative review of a game with so much creative integrity.

Unless somebody can tell me of an overhaul mod that completely reworks the leveling system I just can't reccomend this game in good conscious. A masterpiece in almost every other regard.

I loved Morrowind. I don't like Oblivion. It's not that the world is bad or the story uninteresting, it's the small things that add up giving a bad experience. And I'm sure some people actually like some of the bad points I'm going to list now.

For the record I did the main quest of Oblivion and almost finished the main quest of Shivering Isles at the time of writing. Shivering Isles is a better world and story in my opinion and has some pretty interesting quests. If Oblivion was like this all around I would most likely recommend the game despite its flaws.

* The leveling system is atrocious. After reading about it I decided to do the game without leveling. Trying to level properly requires way too much preparation and thinking.
* All dialogues have voices. It's no longer possible to just skim through an NPC's text, you have to click line by line if you want to skip them and if you missed something important, too bad.
* Related, because all dialogues have voices it feels like a lot of details are lost. Many NPCs don't have much background as a result.
* Related, there's a tiny amount of voices so they get really boring after a while.
* NPCs have daily routines. It's both a blessing and a curse. It's not the best idea when it comes to trainers or other special interactions since the option won't even show up if you speak to them at the wrong time. Night time is largely boring since everyone is sleeping.
* It's way too easy to hit or kill an NPC that's following you. The problem is much worse during some of the larger battles where you basically can't try to fight alongside everyone else or use your best spells and weapons.
* The UI is atrocious. Console-friendly perhaps, but still. Also all the buttons and choices being located on the left is annoying when using a mouse.
* You can't levitate in this game. This was a huge disappointment.
* Oblivion gates are completely boring and there's so many of them that it's not even worth saving the world after a while.
* The scenery doesn't change much and is not all that interesting to begin with (except in Shivering Isles). Many places look too much the same like castles, towns or even some dungeons.
* Even with the unofficial patch you're likely to encounter bugs and crashes, it's disappointing. Save often.

Mods fix a number of these problems but not everything. A positive is that the battle system is superior to Morrowind, but it remains pretty meh, at least without mods to improve it.

Of course everyone already knows that few persons recorded all the spoken dialogues in-game. So you hear usually the same 5 or so voices all the time, talking dumb things like "I always buy things at [insert city name] trader because they have good prices".

Everytime you enter the Oblivion plane, you will see basically the same stuff and behave in the same manner.

I finally got through the whole thing. Though I'm still disappointed by the weaker combat (in terms of role playing) and the dumbed systems, the game has wider appeal and I can appreciate why people like this game over Morrowind and Daggerfall. 
I player Oblivion for the first time when I was in middle school, and when I played it my first reaction was a gutteral disgust at how the soul was completely sucked from the game. Morrowind was dark, alien and interesting and to see the series step back to the Daggerfall aesthetic and be so unabashedly conventional fantasy just kicked the wind out of my interest in playing this game. 
For over a decade, I have just always had that hole in my interest that anytime I wanted to give the game a chance, I just became depressed by it's existence and stop. 
But I'm an adult now, I've played Fallout 3 and New Vegas and with the remaster now out, I had a discussion with a friend about the game that said simply "it's just fantasy Fallout 3, just stop comparing it to Morrowind". With that, I was finally able to get over my aparhy towards the game and play the whole thing. 

The story is better than I thought it would be, essentially being a story about the forces of Hell invading the world. While not really original, the added aspect of the magics of the blood of the emperor and how destiny seems to bend around the emperor's line was a an interesting take on it and the ending really paid off the entire story in an interesting and uncertain way that I really liked. 

The game play is essentially a really stilted action game. Not very deep mechanically, mostly just spamming attack. Morrowind knew the combat was stilted so made an entire system based around charging attacks carefully and using the appropriate directional slashes and stabs to overcome your enemy's attacks and defenses so Oblivion's choice to rip out the entire mechanism that made the stilted combat interesting and tense really is a hit against making the combat interesting. 
Spells make a return in a really simplified way without spell casting failures which made it better in Morrowind. I think you can craft spells too, but I never found how you do that. Same with enchanting items, I think it's present but I never found it and just used the games auto enchant items instead which were less deep. 
Finally, the world is full if interesting side tours and quests, and I did the thieves guild line to completion and enjoyed how the questline built on its self and ended with an extremely complex heist that had an emotional tie sort of shoehorned in at the end. Other quests I played were also just fine, nothing really memorable but that's how it sometimes. 
I think I'll give Skyrim another chance, but with an even more dumbed down game, I'm not sure I'll be able to enjoy it.

Here are a few points about the game that I would like to address:

1: The main story is about you having to help an empire find a new heir for a murdered emperor, but all the known heirs have been killed by a cult. Fortunately, there is a bastard who carries the king's blood, only the secretive Blades know where this man lives so you have to do pick-up and delivery work here and there. You see you are actually more of a side character for a game that likes to work with prophecies. 

2: You have a lot of sidequests that you can have fun with supposedly. I honestly had fun with a handful of quests on it like: 
- You help a paranoid resident of a town spy on his neighbors to find out if there's a plot against him. 
- You can join several guilds, but the most interesting out of all the guilds is the Dark Brotherhoods
- You have to investigate on a missing daughter of a merchant who was last seen in a grimly isolated village.
And I could go on and on. Largely quests are either chasing a bounty, picking up a valuable item in 1 or other ruin with traps or pick up and delivery, nothing unique.

3. The theme of Oblivion has a generic fantasy setting. All of the scenery looks pretty sparse too, during your journey from one point to another you're going to have a path for the most part, lots of green grass and trees occasionally you'll run into a bandit or a monster. Locations are more or less: abandoned/fallen fortresses, caves, ancient elvish ruins and inns. All places follow the same pattern, they all look alike and offer no other interesting ways to take on a mission when they take place in 1 of the copycat places. Nothing feels unique. At one point, for a particular quest at 10 ruins, I had to collect 10 ancient elvish statues for a collector. I raced through each ruin because it felt more like a boring ride since they all looked alike without more challenge. In addition, later in the game you also encounter gates of Oblivion and when you enter them, you find yourself in a volcanic landscape inhabited by demonic creatures. And this is going to keep repeating itself until you finish the main story.

Its predecessor had a better and interesting setting precisely because the island of Vvardenfell looked extraordinary, it was a volcanic landscape with alien-like flora and fauna with dark chilly elves as inhabitants who didn't have it in for foreigners and with a more interesting main story. But I won't delve into that.

Oblivion, at its heart, is a good game. It does some things better than Morrowind/Skyrim, and some things worse (namely, non stealth-archer combat). Overall, it is a [i]pretty fun[/i] Elder Scrolls game.

The problem, is that the engine for Oblivion is absolute trash, to put it mildly. Even if you are wanting a pure "vanilla" experience with no mods, you are not going to have a good time. You need many mods, 3rd party tools, and unofficial patches just to get a [b]SEMI[/b] stable experience. No matter what you do though, you will be besieged by crashes that increase over time.

The pros tell you not to use autosaves or quicksaves. They'll tell you to never overwrite a previous save. They'll say to restart the game after every death. They'll tell you a hundred other tips and tricks that ultimately decrease the enjoyment of your gaming experience.

I cannot count how many times I had to re-do a quest because I kept forgetting to "save manually", and then had a crash right before I thought about saving, or times where I died and just decided not to re-open the game. It's exhausting just how much you have to go through just to play the game.

And even if you follow every instruction and every best practice, you will still, inevitably, lose your savefile to corruption. I've tried on multiple occasions to get a solid "stable" experience going. I've dumped hundreds of hours into Morrowind, Skyrim, and even Oblivion back in the old days. I had hoped that with all my newfound knowledge and experience of these engines, combined with over a decade of community support, that it would be easy to "not screw it up" and get another hundred hours out of from Oblivion.

Attempt #1: Complete and total Savefile corruption after 35 hours.
Attempt #2: Complete and total Savefile corruption after 50 hours.

At the moment of this review, I have 85 hours in Oblivion. I have easily spent more than that trying to research and stabilize a mod list that would maximize the performance, stability, and gameplay aspects of Oblivion. I am feeling very burnt out and disappointed with the end result. I may try and go back to an older save to recover it, but I've done this several times already and I don't have high hopes.

Oblivion has not aged as well as I thought it would, it’s a very average game that has a lot of issues. Playing Oblivion again made me realize how broken the game really is. The biggest issue by far is the level scaling where all the enemies level up with you. You start out fighting mud crabs, rats and goblins and by the end of the game you're still fighting mud crabs that have leveled up with you, but the rats and goblins have mysteriously disappeared to be replaced with ogres and trolls. You start out finding iron and steel swords and face bandits with fur and leather armour. You finish by finding countless ebony weapons and face superbandits with daedric armour. It’s crazy how bad they f*cked this up. Your character could be level 50 that has the best gear and all his stats maxed out and every enemy in a new dungeon you enter will be ogres that are also level 50 and kill you in a few hits. There is no sense of progression and that kills the game in a big way. The fixed enemies in Morrowind for example added tension and reward to the dungeons and the world exploration because you are never sure how strong the enemy will be when you enter a new area which creates a tense atmosphere. But in oblivion there is always the reassurance no matter where you go that the enemy will be on the same level as you which makes all the enemy encounters boring and very dull. A would perfect game is plagued by the issues that you will inevitably face from start to finish. Just as with any Bethesda game, mods are REQUIRED for a smooth and consistent experience. The game suffers from horrendous "micro-stutters" that are present regardless of hardware or actual frame rate. Also on par with any Bethesda release is the ever present "crash-to-desktop" issues. With or without mods, the game will crash and it usually happens in the open world areas where you may not have saved for a long time. While mods can help mitigate these crashes, they are nearly impossible to get rid of completely. Next, quests often bug out as well, either randomly or due to the order in which you have played other quests. This can result in certain quest lines being unplayable without console commands or mods. Finally, if you have played approximately 250 hours on a single save file on PC or approximately 500 hours on a single save file on console, you will encounter the "A-Bomb" glitch which renders that save unplayable without the use of a sketchy save file editor. This glitch causes animations to stop working which means you cannot open doors! Bethesda said, over a decade ago, that they were aware of the "A-Bomb" glitch and that they were working on a fix. Here we are in 2021 without a patch in sight. 

I realize that many people wish to mod Oblivion until it's almost a completely different game but mods SHOULD NOT be a requirement to play the game smoothly and in its vanilla state. Of course I might be able to forgive many of these flaws if they weren't still releasing this same broken product on new platforms every few years. This version of Oblivion has been released at retail, on Steam, GOG, and most recently the Microsoft Store via Gamepass...fifteen years after its initial release. Seriously, how hard is it to task a couple of your devs to fix the game breaking issues on games you are still selling. 343 Industries was able to restore Halo 1 to its original state from nearly 20 years ago when it was broken by a separate developer.

Some other little nitpicky things: No native gamepad support even though the code for it is in game and mods can restore some of its functionality. No achievements on any platform other than the Xbox 360 version. And finally, for the love of god Bethesda stop making video settings locked to the launcher. In-game resolution changes have been a thing since before Morrowind, so please figure this out for your future games.

Among all the mainline Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion stands out as the black sheep in many ways. As is usual with post-Redguard Bethesda, all gameplay elements that don't fully work are quickly removed or wildly simplified. While this serves some games well, such as Morrowind where this approach is balanced with new elements added or Skyrim where the whole experience is as simple as to be a breeze to flow through, Oblivion falls in the awkward middle. Its rpg mechanics are convoluted and have to be grinded against throughout the experience, yet they don't have a payoff and often serve no real purpose. The core gameplay of Oblivion is all fat and no substance. Furthermore, on a purely thematic level, everything in the game barring the main quest, is extremely shallow. While trivial, the writing in general is not fun and self-aware in a youthful and playful way. Instead, to put it bluntly, the writers reveal themselves as simpletons. Multiple questlines are an incoherent and substanceless busywork, while the fabled Dark Brotherhood one is an impressively off-puting and pretentious monument to kitsch. Mr. Pagliarulo might just be the worst writer in the main Bethesda team by far. Hopefully they don't give him the reins to design future games as a whole. Gameplay and writing concerns only make two parts of The Elder Scrolls trifecta - the last being the world design. Unfortunately, even in this corner, there is not much to praise. Since Daggerfall the only game where Bethesda used procedural generation in their mainline games is Oblivion, and it very much shows. Even with mods to rectify the soulless and baffling areas of the map, approximately half of it, Oblivion still manages to have the most underwhelming world amongst all Elder Scrolls games. On the positive side, the game features a fine main quest and Knights of the Nine questline, but these are mere moments in an otherwise painful and insulting experience. Oblivion can only be recommended to hardcore Elder Scrolls fans for a one-off novel playthrough. Or alternatively to bored gamers who want to waste their time away running around bland forests whacking healthsponge enemies for no reason at all. In conclusion, Oblivion just doesn't come together as a coherent product and is by far the worst game Bethesda produced since the mid 90s. Until Starfield, maybe.

But also (and just as important in a Bethesda game), the writing of it's world building is uninspired; the Imperials and Cyrodiil don't stand out in any way from not only other fantasy series, but even from the Bretons or Nords of The Elder Scrolls. Sure, their ancient history is interesting - but this game isn't about their ancient history, it's about their here and now. Ancient minotaurs as guardians of the empire? That's very cool! What the minotaurs you actually find in-game like? Mindless enemies, only distinct because of their appearance.

Lastly (and arguably of least importance), the modding community is smallest of any "modern" TES game, and it seems to be the least stable and expansive game in terms of modding that Bethesda has released since the first Construction Kit.

[h1]A Painful Reflection on Bethesda and Todd Howard[/h1]

As a long-time fan of the Elder Scrolls series, it pains me to write a negative review for [i]The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion[/i]. This game offered an outstanding world full of adventures and stories. The quests were thoughtful and engaging, and the gameplay provided a freedom that was revolutionary at the time. The game received high praise and became a benchmark for open-world RPGs.

[h2]Bethesda's Decline[/h2]

Sadly, when I look at the current state of Bethesda Softworks and Todd Howard, I cannot hide my disappointment. Once, Bethesda stood for quality and innovation. Todd Howard was a developer who turned his passion for games into masterpieces like [i]Oblivion[/i] and [i]Morrowind[/i]. These games offered depth and immersion that were unparalleled.

However, the tide has turned. A stark example is the release of [i]Fallout 76[/i] in 2018. The game was universally panned by critics and players alike. Technical issues, outdated graphics, and a lack of meaningful content were just a few of the criticisms. Despite a reduced price and various updates, the game failed to meet expectations, receiving a user score of only 2.7/10 on Metacritic.

While [i]Oblivion[/i] and [i]Skyrim[/i] sold millions of copies and made Bethesda a giant in the gaming industry, the recent years have shown significant cracks in the company’s image. From 2017 to 2020, Bethesda's revenue grew from $7.8 billion to $10.4 billion, with much of this growth attributed to aggressive monetization strategies rather than the quality of their games.

[h2]Economic Realities and Game Development Costs[/h2]

Developing a game like [i]The Elder Scrolls VI[/i] requires a massive investment. According to industry reports, developing a AAA game can cost between $60 million and $100 million, not including marketing expenses which can double the total cost. In contrast, mobile games often require a fraction of this budget, sometimes as low as $1 million to $5 million. This stark difference in investment highlights why studios might prefer the lower-risk, higher-reward model of mobile games over expansive, high-budget titles.

In 2020, the global mobile gaming market was valued at approximately $77.2 billion, outpacing the revenue generated by PC and console games combined. This lucrative market has driven many studios, including Bethesda, to focus more on mobile and live-service games that can continuously generate revenue through microtransactions.

[h2]Challenges in Talent Acquisition and Retention[/h2]

Another significant challenge in the current gaming industry is attracting and retaining top talent. The demand for skilled developers, artists, and designers has skyrocketed, and the competition among companies is fierce. Talented individuals are often lured away by tech giants like Google and Amazon, which offer more lucrative compensation packages and benefits.

Moreover, the gaming industry has faced scrutiny over workplace culture and crunch time, leading to burnout and high turnover rates among employees. This environment makes it difficult for studios to maintain a stable and experienced workforce, which in turn affects the quality of the games produced. When compared to the early 2000s, the landscape of game development has changed dramatically, with talent being more scattered and less loyal to a single company for long periods.

[h2]Todd Howard: From Visionary to Businessman[/h2]

Todd Howard, once a visionary developer, now seems more interested in maximizing profits than creating epic, high-quality games. His earlier works reflected his passion and dedication, but recent releases suggest that the focus has shifted more towards quick profits than lasting enjoyment.

The release of [i]Fallout 76[/i] highlights this change. Despite numerous promises and apologies, the game remained far from expectations. This indicates a shift in priorities at Bethesda. Instead of crafting new and exciting game worlds, it appears the main goal is finding the next big revenue stream.

[h2]A Wake-Up Call for Gamers[/h2]

For us as gamers, this is a bitter wake-up call. We need to critically assess our expectations and trust in future projects from Bethesda. It is disheartening to see a company and its leading developer, who once stood for quality and innovation, abandon their ideals in favor of profit maximization.

The glory days of Bethesda, when they developed games like [i]Oblivion[/i] and [i]Skyrim[/i], seem to be over. It is time for us as a community to raise our voices and demand that developers return to their roots – to a time when it was about telling epic stories and creating unforgettable gaming experiences.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

Bethesda and Todd Howard must decide whether to continue on the path of quick money or return to the principles that once made them so successful. Until then, we should be cautious before investing in their games again.

The controls feel horrible. They're floaty, awkward, janky. Combat is a mishmash of swiveling back and forth uncontrollably, and your blows are stunted while feeling weightless, magic is sluggish to unresponsive, so all in all you won't know what's going on while you're trying in vain to avoid getting killed. 

As for the RPG mechanics, ugh. The pacing is positively inept. You've got the oily action RPG mechanics competing with the drudgery of an obliquely intrusive leveling system that punishes you for bonus stat mechanics so arbitrary that it can only be reasoned they're intentionally malevolent. Why add further stats upon skills when what matters in the end is how suited your character is to a task? Why bother with a middleman at all? What justification is other than to make the game seem unnecessarily more "RPG-esque"? 

The presentation isn't much better. The graphics are atrocious, and not by modern standards. For no justifiable reason, Argonians look like they vomited pixels on a potato. Khajiit look vaguely normal because there's only a slight effect like they're being sucked through a vacuum located in front of your monitor. The other races are just different skintones of humans and humans with pointy ears, as if they just ran out of ideas on how to make their fantasy game actually fantastic. You can't justify this by saying, "Oh, that's the best our hardware can manage until the future". You have to look at this and realize it doesn't look anything like it's meant to.
